# Asking for resources (and why over-asking punishes you) {#sec-resources}

::: {.tldr}
Ask for what your job actually needs — cores, memory, time — and no more. Every extra core,
gigabyte, or hour makes your job **harder to schedule**, so it waits longer, and it burns more
of your allocation. Over-asking hurts *you* first. Two rules: **always set `--mem`
explicitly**, and **measure real usage with `seff` after your first run**, then right-size.
:::

## Cores, tasks, and the words Slurm uses

Slurm's vocabulary is a little fussy, but for most jobs you only need two ideas:

- A **task** is one instance of your program. Most jobs are a single task.
- **CPUs per task** is how many cores that program can use (its threads).

```bash
#SBATCH --nodes=1                # keep a job on one node unless it's true MPI
#SBATCH --ntasks=1               # one program instance
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8        # that can use 8 cores
```

- **Single-threaded program?** `--ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=1`.
- **Multithreaded (OpenMP, most numpy/xarray work)?** `--ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=N`, and
  set `export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK`.
- **MPI across many nodes?** Use `--nodes` and `--ntasks`, and launch with `srun` (@sec-ladder).

Asking for 8 cores does **not** make a single-threaded program faster — it just reserves 7
idle cores and makes you wait longer. Match the request to what your code can actually use.

## Memory — the directive people forget, then regret

Set memory explicitly, every time. Two ways:

```bash
#SBATCH --mem=32G              # total memory for the whole job (simplest)
# or
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=4G       # memory per core (scales with --cpus-per-task)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Remember the 10 GB/core default on `mb`
If you omit `--mem` on the default partition, you get **10 GB per core**, so
`--cpus-per-task=8` silently becomes a 80 GB request. That queues slower and can be rejected
outright if it exceeds a limit. Name your memory. (Full story in @sec-anatomy.)
:::

How much do you actually need? For a first run, estimate high-ish so it doesn't get killed,
then **measure and right-size** (below). A job that exceeds its memory request is killed by
the out-of-memory (OOM) killer (@sec-fail) — so memory is the one resource where running out
is fatal rather than merely slow.

## Time — long enough to finish, short enough to start

```bash
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00        # HH:MM:SS  (or D-HH:MM:SS, e.g. 2-00:00:00)
```

Your job is **killed the instant it hits this limit**, so the request must exceed the real
runtime — pad by, say, 25%. But don't pad wildly: a shorter time limit means a **lower QOS
ceiling and better odds of backfilling into gaps**, so it often *starts sooner*
(@sec-queue-times). There's a real tension here, and picking the time limit thoughtfully is
one of the highest-leverage things you do.

::: {.callout-note}
## There is no per-partition default time — so set `--time`
Partitions on MedicineBow don't set a default wall time. If you don't specify `--time`, you
inherit the partition maximum (7 days), which your QOS will then likely reject (the `normal`
QOS caps at 3 days). Always set `--time` yourself so the job's request is coherent.
:::

## Over-asking punishes you first

It's worth making this concrete, because it's counterintuitive to newcomers:

- **More cores / memory** → fewer nodes can satisfy you → **longer wait**, and you're
  charged for cores you didn't use.
- **More time** → lower-priority QOS tier and fewer backfill opportunities → **longer wait**.
- **A GPU you don't use** → you sit in the (busy) GPU queue for nothing (@sec-queue-times).

The scheduler isn't punishing you on purpose; a bigger, longer request is simply a rarer set
of free resources to find. The lesson: **right-size**.

## Measure, then right-size, with `seff`

After a job finishes, `seff` tells you what it actually used versus what you reserved:

```bash
seff 123456
```

```text
Job ID: 123456
State: COMPLETED
Cores: 8
CPU Efficiency: 24.13% of 04:16:00 core-walltime      <- you used ~2 of 8 cores
Memory Utilized: 5.31 GB
Memory Efficiency: 16.59% of 32.00 GB                 <- 32G reserved, 5G used
```

Read that as: *next time ask for ~2 cores and ~8 GB.* Low CPU efficiency means you reserved
cores your code can't use; low memory efficiency means you can ask for far less and start
sooner. One measured run is worth a dozen guesses.

Check what you're even *allowed* to ask for with ARCC's helper:

```bash
showuserlimits
```

Now that you can size a job, the next decision is *where* to send it — partitions and QOS,
and the queue-time consequences of each (@sec-partitions, @sec-queue-times).
